summary: This experimental document describes Compressed Bundle Header Encoding, a convention for convergence-layer adapters to represent endpoint identifiers compactly in the primary block of DTN bundles. It works when the identifiers follow a prescribed structure.

plainLanguage.summary: Compressed Bundle Header Encoding shortens some endpoint identifiers in a DTN bundle header. Both communicating convergence-layer adapters must support the encoding, and the bundle must meet its format rules.

questions: how to shrink dtn endpoint ids
what is the ipn uri scheme
how does dtn header compression work
subtitle: A constrained encoding that replaces DTN endpoint strings with integer pairs.

tldr.problem: A Bundle Protocol primary block stores endpoint identifiers as strings, which can make a small bundle's header large.
tldr.mechanism: When all four endpoint IDs and the dictionary meet the required constraints, a convergence-layer adapter replaces their offsets with eight integers and omits the dictionary.
tldr.outcome: The receiving adapter must reconstruct the ordinary primary block before passing it to bundle processing. RFC 6260 is Experimental and is updated by RFC 9758.

today: RFC 6260 is an Experimental RFC from the IRTF and is updated by RFC 9758. Its status note says it was published for examination, experimental implementation, and evaluation.

sections.title: Why Compress a Bundle Header
sections.content:
The Bundle Protocol primary block contains identifiers for the source, destination, report-to endpoint, and current custodian. The block uses a dictionary of scheme names and scheme-specific parts, with offsets that identify those strings.

Even with that dictionary, endpoint strings can take up a large part of a bundle when its payload is small. CBHE is a convergence-layer adaptation that reduces this header information. Bundle processing sees the usual form after the receiver reconstructs it.
sections.plainLanguage: A bundle header stores several endpoint identifiers as text. CBHE can replace those strings with shorter values before transmission.

sections.title: The ipn Endpoint Identifier
sections.content:
CBHE can encode only the null endpoint ID dtn:none or an endpoint ID using the ipn URI scheme. An ipn identifier contains a node number, a period, and a service number, as in ipn:9.37.

The node number ranges from 1 to 2^64 minus 1. The service number ranges from 0 to 2^64 minus 1. Node number zero is reserved to represent the null endpoint in compressed form; decompression must turn it back into dtn:none.
sections.plainLanguage: An ipn endpoint identifier has a node number and a service number separated by a period. The service number helps direct a bundle to the intended application function.

sections.title: When a Dictionary Can Be Compressed
sections.content:
All endpoint identifiers in a bundle's primary block must be CBHE-conformant. The dictionary must also follow a specified order: destination strings first, followed by source, report-to, and custodian strings only when each differs from strings already included.

A bundle cannot be compressed if an extension block refers to another endpoint identifier that would add a string to the dictionary. These constraints let the receiver reconstruct the dictionary from the integer values.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression works only for specified endpoint identifiers and a dictionary in the required order. Extra endpoint references prevent the receiver from rebuilding the dictionary.

sections.title: Replacing and Rebuilding the Dictionary
sections.content:
When sending a qualifying bundle, the convergence-layer adapter replaces the eight scheme-name and scheme-specific-part offsets with node and service number pairs. The order is destination, source, report-to, then current custodian. Null endpoint IDs are represented by zero values, and the dictionary length is set to zero.

A CBHE-capable receiving adapter recognizes a zero dictionary length and must decompress the primary block before delivering the bundle to the bundle protocol agent. A sender may compress only when the receiver is known or presumed to understand CBHE.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender substitutes eight numbers for the dictionary offsets and marks the dictionary as empty. The receiving adapter reconstructs the ordinary endpoint identifiers before bundle processing.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability Limits
sections.content:
Some Bundle Security Protocol extension blocks add endpoint identifiers to the dictionary. If those identifiers are outside the four primary-block endpoints, the bundle does not meet CBHE's dictionary constraint and cannot be compressed.

The RFC also describes a denial-of-service risk if a receiver trusts a compressed bundle's claimed source to infer that the sender supports CBHE. It suggests requiring Bundle Authentication Blocks and not inferring support from unauthenticated bundles.
sections.plainLanguage: Some security extensions add identifiers that prevent compression. Authentication can also help stop a false sender identity from causing a receiver to use CBHE with an incompatible peer.
